before.text: Put one drop of food coloring into a glass of water.
Without stirring, it spreads through the whole glass.
Wait as long as you like, and it never gathers back into a drop.
The usual explanation is entropy, often called disorder.
But what is entropy, really?
Roll two dice: the total is like a macrostate, and each exact pair of faces is like a microstate.
Seven can be made six ways, but two only one way, so seven turns up six times as often.
Entropy is that kind of count: how many microstates make the same macrostate.
Now the real thing: a box of gas with a left half and a right half.
What we see, gas filling the whole box, is the macrostate.
One exact arrangement of every molecule's position and energy is a microstate.
Shrink the box to four molecules, and there are sixteen microstates.
Only one of them puts all four in the left half.
But six of them put two molecules in each half.
So spread evenly beats all on the left six to one, just like seven beats two on the dice.
Back in the full box, picture a hundred molecules.
What are the odds of catching them all in the left half at one moment?
Less than one in a million trillion trillion.
The molecules move randomly, so the gas ends up spread out, the macrostate with by far the most microstates.
That's the second law of thermodynamics: the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
An isolated system is one that trades no energy or matter with its surroundings.
Now, a common mistake is to think entropy simply means disorder.
Entropy counts microstates, so it measures how widely energy and particles are spread, not how messy things look.
Now, why does hot coffee cool down in a cool room?
When heat flows into something, its entropy rises by the heat divided by its absolute temperature.
Heat leaves the coffee at a higher temperature and enters the room at a lower one.
Dividing by the smaller temperature gives a bigger result, so the room gains more entropy than the coffee loses.
Total entropy rises, and that's why heat flows on its own from hot to cold.
So entropy counts the ways particles and energy can be arranged, and nature drifts toward states with the most ways.
It isn't disorder: it's the number of microstates behind what you see, and it's why the drop never gathers back.
